comments.author: jacquesm
comments.text:
I've owned 1x2cV, 3xDS/ID (one a donor car), 2x Xantia and 1 XM. All of them had something that very few modern cars have, which is that they were quirky but interesting, both technology wise and to drive. If you knew them well you could do just about anything with them.
Anyway, about that hydraulic system: a friend of mine who lived in IJmuiden was improving his house. To do so he had bought a load of concrete tiles in Amsterdam on an impulse (really, really good deal). So he called me up and asked if I could come and help shift them to IJmuiden. When I got there there was this absolutely massive pile and I figured this is not going to end well. I had dropped the rear seat (which you could pull out fairly easily, but the back cushions stayed in place) so there was quite a bit of room and two tiles fit side by side. So we stacked them pretty much to the ceiling and miraculously, the car just kept on adjusting ride height and never gave any sign that it couldn't handle the load. All of the tiles fit. Then we drove to IJmuiden. It all went well until we hit the overpass over the road between Amsterdam and Haarlem on A9. The car took a bit of a dive into the dip and then came back out

comments.author: Squeeeez
comments.text: I still remember having to wait for the car to rise, as a child. Didn't know how smooth my rides were until we switched from citroen to renault. But the hydraulic system membranes seem to have needed extensive maintenance, quite sad. Mechanics didn't love them.

comments.author: Svip
comments.text:
Generally goes unnoticed (though not unmentioned), but until after the Xantia, the suspension system also included the brakes and the steering (which would technically not be permitted under modern EU car standards); which meant a leak would eventually not just cause a loss of suspension, but also a loss of steering and braking.
Why incorporate the braking and the suspension?  The mechanical height regulator could "feel" how much fluid it needed to fill the suspension with, in order to obtain the desired ride height; which meant it "knew" how heavy the vehicle was loaded, and thus apply the brakes accordingly.  This is why in a proper Citroën hydraulic car, the brake pedal feels "weird", in that it doesn't go far down (and quickly becomes hard to press) (the DS tried to make this less confusion by making the pedal a "mushroom" button instead); because the idea is that you should apply gentle braking, and the car will figure out the necessary amount of braking force required (unlike just hitting the pedal like in a normal car, which would result in an almost hard stop).
Why the steering then?  I think that's more of a convenience thing, mechanically speaking, as it was already there

There’s a concept called the Deflection Dilemma (or the Sagan-Ostro Dilemma, after its creators), which argues that because we’d likely have enough advance warning to deflect a dangerous asteroid on an impact course, we should build the tech just-in-time rather than in advance. The argument is about dual-use risk: any technology capable of deflecting near-Earth objects (NEOs) away from Earth could also be used to redirect harmless ones toward us, and that humans are just irrational enough to actually do it.
I used to think the psychological part of the idea was weak, like why would anyone intentionally steer an asteroid into Earth? But the movie `Don’t Look Up` convinced me that a scenario where companies try to nudge asteroids closer to mine rare-earth minerals is plausible. Given how AI development is going, I think we should probably treat asteroid-deflection tech with the same caution we apply to nuclear or AI capabilities.

It’s taken some time to process but LCC strikes me as remarkably observant and child-like in certain ways - “flat-lying” vs “sharp-lying” tonal relationships, classifying congruity/incongruity of melody vs. the harmony underneath, and the ordering of “ingoing” and “outgoing” tones.
The most useful insight in the whole experience was the “tonal gravity chart” - a fold-out mapping of some of the above. I can’t recall if it was an insert in the published text or something we were given as an addendum.
Russell’s willingness to essentially ignore the horizontal tension-release expectations and consider harmony in terms of pure sound and vertical slices of time was refreshing, though it was easy to be led astray by his voluminous assumptions and beliefs. One composition teacher where I studied dissuaded his students from taking the course, believing it “ruined” composers. Going all-in on LCC never really seemed to work for anybody but George and a handful of his students.
